candidates.question: Did David pay in silver or gold?

side_b.label: Six hundred shekels of gold

candidates.summary_60_seconds: Samuel says David paid fifty shekels of silver for the threshing floor and oxen. Chronicles says he paid six hundred shekels of gold for the place. Both the metal and the amount differ in the accounts of this purchase. But the descriptions of what he bought are also different. A larger piece of land in Chronicles could allow two payments for different parts of the purchase. Neither book explicitly reports two payments, so that remains a possible explanation. The record does not rely on the owner's different names in the two books. It also does not claim that the KJV changed the amounts from the Hebrew text. The central question is whether the prices cover the same property. The passages alone do not settle the boundaries of what each payment bought.
candidates.what_would_settle_it: Establish whether the payments cover different property; neither book explicitly reports the proposed two-payment explanation for the differing amounts.
candidates.why_selected: The price gap is clear, but another census question already gives David’s story a place among the thirty.

record_provenance.scope_verbatim: Samuel names what was bought as “the threshingfloor and the oxen” and Chronicles as “the place”. The KJV matches the Hebrew in each book, and Brenton’s Greek of 2 Samuel 24:24 also has fifty shekels of silver, so no tag is proposed. candidates.question: Did Michal bear five sons or raise them?

side_a.label: The KJV says she brought them up

side_b.label: The cited Hebrew and Greek say she bore them
side_b.reference_note: The KJV says brought up here; this side uses the Hebrew and old Greek translation described in the record.

candidates.summary_60_seconds: The KJV says Michal brought up five sons for Adriel. The Hebrew text and old Greek translation cited by the record instead say she bore them. Another passage says Michal had no child until her death. A further passage names Merab, rather than Michal, as the woman given to Adriel. The translation choice therefore affects how readers see the relationship between these statements. Raising children need not mean giving birth to them, so the KJV wording removes that part of the conflict. It still names Michal in the passage. The record does not decide whether her name resulted from a copying mistake. The editions cited both name Michal and do not establish what every ancient copy contains. The translators' source for their wording also remains unestablished by this comparison.
candidates.what_would_settle_it: Compare evidence for the name and wording; the record establishes neither a copying mistake nor the translators’ source here.
candidates.why_selected: A family question exposes a meaningful translation difference; it remains a reserve because Goliath already introduces this type of comparison.

record_provenance.scope_verbatim: The KJV wording removes the conflict with 2 Samuel 6:23 but still names Michal rather than Merab. No claim is made about whether “Michal” in the Hebrew is a copying slip for “Merab”; the named Hebrew and Greek editions both print Michal. The Greek agrees with the Hebrew against the KJV, so both H and G apply. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined, and the KJV translators’ source for their wording is not established here. candidates.question: Did Noah board before the flood or that day?

side_a.label: Entry followed by a seven-day interval

side_b.label: Entry on the flood’s starting day

candidates.summary_60_seconds: Genesis first describes Noah entering the ark and then says the floodwaters came after seven days. A later passage dates the flood's beginning and places Noah's entry on that same day. Reading each sentence as the next event creates a difference in the timing. The record also preserves other ways of reading the account. The earlier entry could be a summary that the later passage expands. The same-day wording could mark the day the whole boarding process was complete. Those possibilities prevent the draft from treating sentence order as the only possible timeline. The record makes no Hebrew or Greek comparison for this finding. It also does not confirm that a flood occurred. This is a question about the surviving narrative's order, separate from the science candidate about a recent worldwide event.
candidates.what_would_settle_it: Clarify whether the entries are a summary and expansion or mark completion; the record preserves both possible readings here.
candidates.why_selected: A clear timing puzzle offers a textual reserve, while the recommended flood candidate addresses external scientific evidence instead.

record_provenance.scope_verbatim: Genesis 7:7 may be read as a summary that is expanded in 7:13, and “selfsame day” can mark the day the whole embarkation was complete. These readings are preserved. The record is a comparison of the surviving narrative, not confirmation of a flood. No Hebrew or Greek comparison was made, so no H or G tag is proposed.

candidates.question: Who laid the foundation: Sheshbazzar or Zerubbabel?

side_b.label: Zerubbabel in the work account and prophecy

candidates.summary_60_seconds: Ezra reports an answer from the elders that credits Sheshbazzar with laying the temple foundation. Another passage names Zerubbabel and Jeshua as starting the work, then says builders laid the foundation. Zechariah directly credits Zerubbabel's hands with laying it. The statements give credit in different ways, but the record keeps two possible links open. Sheshbazzar and Zerubbabel could be two names for one man. Both could also have played a part, with one in charge and another doing the work. None of the quoted verses gives either explanation. The claims also come from different speakers, including an answer within a reported letter. That matters when deciding who says what. The record does not prove which man did the physical work. It also does not settle how the two names are related.
candidates.what_would_settle_it: Establish whether the names identify one person or shared roles; the quoted passages state neither proposed explanation for the difference.
candidates.why_selected: This broadens the book mix, but long names and shared roles make it less direct than the recommended text comparisons.

record_provenance.scope_verbatim: No tag is proposed: in each verse the KJV follows the Hebrew or Aramaic quoted, and Brenton’s Greek names the same men. The statements can both stand if Sheshbazzar and Zerubbabel are two names of one man, or if both had a part in the laying, one as the governor in charge and one as the builder on the ground; no verse quoted says either. Ezra 5:16 is the elders’ answer as Tatnai’s letter reports it, not the narrator’s own statement. Ezra 3:10 says “the builders” laid the foundation and does not name Zerubbabel in that clause. A whole-word search of the packaged KJV finds “Sheshbazzar” at Ezra 1:8, 1:11, 5:14 and 5:16 only; that is a word search, not a reading of every book. candidates.question: Do the dead stay inactive or wake again?

side_a.label: The dead take no part in life under the sun

side_b.label: The dead awaken in Daniel’s vision

candidates.summary_60_seconds: Ecclesiastes describes the dead as taking no further part in what happens under the sun. It speaks of a place of the dead without work or knowledge. Daniel instead describes people awakening from death in a vision. The passages conflict if the first account denies every possible future life. But its repeated focus on earthly life allows another reading. Present inactivity could be different from a future awakening. Under that reading, the two passages need not speak about the same time or condition. The record preserves this distinction rather than deciding that one account rules out the other. It compares two kinds of writing and what their statements may mean. It does not offer tested evidence for or against life after death. This reserve broadens the range of books without changing that limit.
candidates.what_would_settle_it: Clarify whether Ecclesiastes denies all future life or describes present inactivity; the record does not verify an afterlife.
candidates.why_selected: This broadens the book mix, but the contrast depends on whether the passages describe the same time after death.

record_provenance.scope_verbatim: Literary comparison, not empirical verification of an afterlife.
